en: Kṣemendra: *Kalāvilāsa* There is a vast city, a sacred abode of auspiciousness embraced by the touch of Kamalā; it is radiant with jewels, like the chest of the Lord of Śrī. (1.1)
There, the serpent Śeṣa, by means of the multitude of pearl-strings suspended from the jeweled floor,
constantly supports the palaces as if dividing himself into many forms.
The multitude of mansions, formidable with their crystalline luster, acts as an obstacle for the women going to meet their lovers;
therein shines the thief who lays bare the veil of nocturnal darkness. // 1.3 //
Where the mind-born [Cupid] survives by acting like a moth in the rows of flames from the fire of the three-eyed god’s eye, sustained by the nectar of the moon-faced woman’s facial radiance.

Where breezes blow, repeatedly carrying droplets of perspiration from women languid and lovely with amorous play, and perfuming the bodies [of men] with the fragrance of flowers from loosened hair. // 1.5 //
Where, in the lotus groves, the sweet warbling of swans— rendered hoarse from devouring mouthfuls of fresh, tender lotus shoots— spreads forth like the tinkling of the anklets of Lakṣmī.
Where there stands a row of emerald water-chambers, with dancing, charming peacocks, resembling the very embodiment of the rainy season, constantly accompanied by masses of clouds bearing rainbows.
There, in crystal palaces draped with moonbeams, the fawn-eyed women shine like Apsarases emerged from the milky waves of the ocean of nectar. // 1.8 //
There lived one named the illustrious Mūladeva, a leader among those who are repositories of all the arts, and a rogue who had mastered hundreds of vast collections of magical illusions.
Possessing immense wealth, he acquired vast riches through his own virtues, like a universal monarch, while being supported by rogues who had come from various directions and lands.
Once, after he had finished his meal, while he was seated in the assembly hall,
a caravan leader approached him and presented precious offerings of jewels and gold.
Having bowed down, Hiraṇyagupta, together with his son Candragupta, received a seat and hospitality; once he had rested for a moment, he spoke.
Through excessive familiarity, this speech of one such as I before you has lost its brilliance; like a rustic woman in a city, it does not attain such boldness.
O radiant one, this mass of rays of wisdom, which eclipses the splendor of Bṛhaspati, dispels the darkness of the quarters like the innate light of the sun. // 1.14 //
"This only son of mine was born to me in my final years, though my treasury is filled with manifold jewels, pearls, and gold accumulated since birth. (1.15)
Childhood is a ground for delusion, and youth is the intoxication of the mind with passion; and accumulations of wealth are as fickle as water upon the lotus leaf trembling in the wind.
Captivating with deer-like eyes, these rogues are constant bees at the lotus of sensual enjoyment;
alas, this succession of faults has fallen upon my son.
For the simple-minded, there is no liberation at all from the balls of rogues, from the jeweled anklets on the feet of courtesans, or from those born in the houses of the wealthy. (1.18)
Those who do not know place or time, whose mouths are restless, and who, though lame, are full of leaps—such fools are devoured by cunning cats like young birds. (1.19)
O learned one, this son of yours who has taken refuge [with you] is truly dearer to you than your own biological son; grant him the highest wisdom so that he does not come to ruin. 1.20

Having heard these well-spoken words uttered by him with his head bowed in humility, Mūladeva, the corners of his lips spread wide with outpourings of affection, spoke to him: iti vinayanamraśirasā tena vaco yuktamuktamavadhārya & tamuvāca mūladevaḥ prītiprasaraiḥ prasāritauṣṭhāgraḥ // 1.21 //
"Let this son of mine remain in my house like his own, devoted to diligent effort;
he shall gradually learn the entire heart of the arts as taught by me. (1.22)
Thus, at his command, the wise caravan leader sent his own son to that man's house; then, having paid homage, he departed for his own home filled with joy.
Then the sun, its web of rays slackened and its luster turned to smoke,
became invisible while still above the horizon, like a gambler defeated by rogues.
When the maker of day had set, the twilight shone before him like the glow of a mass of vermilion, as if clinging to the elephant of dense darkness.
Although she was abandoned day after day, the splendor of the day followed the maker of the day;
yet the twilight, though red with passion, did not follow him. For who truly knows the heart of women?
When the twilight glow had slowly departed somewhere from the lotus-thicket in the courtyard of the sky,
the darkness, wandering like a bee and distressed by its failure to find a resting place, roamed about.
The earth became closed up, as if by darkness, through the delusions of separation from the sun of sharp rays;
for even one who is fierce becomes dear to people when he has always been their companion.
The night shone forth, its beauty enhanced by clusters of pearls that were the exceedingly bright stars;
it was like a Śabara maiden adorned with ornaments made of peacock feathers consisting of dense darkness.
Then there slowly arose the light of the moon, which consumes the wives of travelers,
a messenger for the awakening of the night-lilies, and a heavy burden of calamity for the female cakravāka birds.
The lord of the night shone forth like a white parasol for the god of love, a spotless crystal mirror for the women of the quarters, and a white tilaka mark upon the face of the lady Night.
The moon, white in its luster, shone upon the bank of the celestial river like a royal swan sporting within a circle formed by the creeper-like stalks of its own lotus fibers.

The dark-complexioned woman shone with the moon; by her, the god of love [shone] with the spring festival; and by that festival, the playful grace of the fawn-eyed women, whose minds were intoxicated with passion, [shone]. 1.33.
The clever ministers of prosperity, having abandoned the lusterless lotus pond, joyfully entered the clusters of blossoming night-lilies like bees.

Smiling with moonlight for its ashes, adorned with the beautiful crescent of the moon as its exquisite skull, and wearing a necklace of a multitude of stars for its bones, the night shone like a Kāpālikī ascetic woman.
In that garden of his own jeweled palace, where every quarter was illuminated by the mass of rays from the full moon, he brought his meditative absorption to completion.
Seated upon a crystal throne together with the moon, his inseparable friend,
he sat with the circle of his principal disciples, headed by Kandalin, surrounding the base of his footstool.
Having gazed for a long time at the caravan leader’s son standing before him, Mūladeva spoke,
as if making the moonlight shrink in shame with the rays of his teeth.
Listen, my son, to the exceedingly crooked essence of the heart of all the arts of deceivers, by knowing which even fortunes, as fickle as a flash of lightning, become stable. (1.39)
In this dense thicket of existence, there is a single well covered by a network of grass, shoots, and creepers,
into which bewildered deer fall, finding no support.
This very treasure-pot named hypocrisy stands in the world, naturally profound, its mouth concealed by the crooked serpents of deceit. (1.41)
The secret mantra of illusion is a wish-fulfilling gem for desired objects;
it is the pride that brings power to the cunning and the means of subjugating Fortune.
By whom can the course of the deceitful be known, who is always like a fish in the water?
He has neither hands, nor feet, nor a head; he is truly difficult to perceive.
By the power of mantras serpents are captured, deer by means of deceptive traps, birds by nets spread on the ground, and human beings by hypocrisy. (1.44)
Victorious is Dambha, the deception of people's hearts, the pillar of illusion, the undertaking of world-conquest,
who is himself eternally unperceived, and the source of the arising of all illusory manifestations.
In this vast wheel of the cycle of existence, which revolves with constant whirling and possesses a thousand crooked spokes of unbearable toil, deceit is the hub and hypocrisy is the nave.

The tree of hypocrisy has its root in the closing of the eyes; it is long watered by the moisture from the hair-tuft wet from bathing; it bears flowers of purity and fruits upon hundreds of branches of a hundred pleasures. // 1.47 //
The hypocrisy born of the crane consists in vows and observances; the hypocrisy born of the tortoise consists in concealed observances;
and the terrible hypocrisy born of the cat consists in the restraint of one's gait and gaze. (1.48)
Bakadambha, Dambhapati, Dambhanarendra, Kūrmaja Dambha,
and Mārjāradambha attained the status of universal emperors among deceivers.

With nails, beard, and hair kept short, either shaven-headed or wearing matted locks, or with a long beard; a demon for excessive clay [on his body], speaking sparingly, and careful in his gait. // 1.50 //
With a golden vine placed upon the back of his purificatory cord of thick knots,
and with his arm covered by a cloth-fillet tucked under his armpit, he resembled a man holding a vessel in his hand.

His scholarship was occupied with the finger-snap gestures and the conceptualization of various disputes; his lips were restless with muttered prayers; and he was intent on meditation amidst the crowds in the city streets. (1.52)
At the sacred bathing place, he repeatedly touched the corners of his ears, blocking the entire world from view with ritual sips of water taken in gracefully tilted handfuls and with long immersions.
His winter bath, difficult to endure, was signaled by his whistling and the clashing of his teeth;
his worship of the gods was indicated by the extensive application of tilaka paste, which served as a substitute for all ritual offerings.
One who carries a flower upon his head while acting as if he were casting down a glance like that of a crow—whatever man acts in such a manner, he should be known as a hypocrite. 1.55.
Bowing before those devoid of virtue while being arrogant toward those possessed of virtue, hating his own kinsmen, a friend to the citizens, seeking fame, hypocritical, and a rogue. (1.56)
At the time of utilizing his services, he bows his head and utters hundreds of flatteries; yet once his task is accomplished, he becomes silent, frowning, hypocritical, and cruel. (1.57)
That Daitya who was formerly Jambha, whose prosperity as a god was paralyzed,
is this very Dambha who now dwells upon the surface of the earth within the bodies of living beings.
The hypocrisy of purity, the hypocrisy of tranquility, the hypocrisy of being a graduate student (snātaka), and the hypocrisy of meditative absorption—
even these do not equal a hundredth part of the hypocrisy of one who is free from desire.

This person, who disputes matters of purity and conduct, who causes the depletion of clay, and who touches his own kinsmen under the guise of hypocrisy regarding cleanliness, attains the state of Viśvāmitra.

Having withdrawn many kinds of beings, this submarine fire—whose great thirst for the waters of wealth and possessions is insatiable, whose water is constant non-violence, and which devours everything—is ever-present. (1.61)

Shaven-headed, matted-haired, naked, bearing an umbrella or a staff, clad in saffron robes, or with a body smeared with ashes—the hypocrite expands his influence as a seeker of enjoyments in every direction. (1.62)
Whether he be bald-headed with a stout body or thin-limbed with the appearance of a sage, or one whose head is wrapped in a cloth like the high peak of a reliquary mound; // 1.63 //
Greed is his aged father; Deceit is his mother; Fraud is his brother;
and his wife is Crookedness; the son of Deceit is the sound "Hum. (1.64)
In the past, the Blessed One, the Self-Existent, having created the worlds and the emanation of beings,
remained for a very long time filled with anxiety due to his state of having ceased all activity.

Having seen with his divine vision those mortals in the world of men who were without support, and who, due to their excellence in uprightness and yoga, had not attained the enjoyment of wealth and other such things; // 1.66 //
With eyes closed, he quickly established himself in an illusory meditative absorption and,
for the prosperity of men, created hypocrisy as the foundation for his reputation.
Carrying a bundle of *kuśa* grass, a book, a rosary, and an empty water-pot;
a staff with a crooked tip like his own heart, a black antelope skin, and a digging tool. (1.68)

His ears were marked with very thick kuśa-grass purifiers, his hands held sacred grass, and the roots of his topknot were clearly visible upon his shaven head, adorned with white flowers entwined with kuśa grass. // 1.69 //
With his neck stiff as wood, his lips moving restlessly in recitation, and his eyes absorbed in meditation,
he carried in his hand a rosary of rudrākṣa beads and bore a bowl filled with clay.
With sidelong glances full of anger, with frowns, sounds of "hum," and facial gestures,
and through various kinds of torment, he who remained silent made known the entire desire of his heart.
Desiring purity, he guarded against the touch of others even in the world of Brahmā; yet hypocrisy stood before him, rising up as if longing for a seat.
By his supreme and magnificent attire, even the Seven Sages were suddenly brought under his influence; they stood before him with palms joined in reverence.
Upon seeing him, even Parameṣṭhin—who had brought about the entire range of creation as a mere sport—stood motionless, swayed by gravity, wonder, and joy. (1.74)

While Agastya was being swallowed by him due to his exceedingly intense ascetic discipline, and while Vasiṣṭha—with his back hunched from the shame of his meager vows of austerity—stood as if struck with extreme amazement; (1.75)

When Kautsa was made to shrink from the reproach of having embraced the exceedingly simple vow of a sage, and when Nārada was rendered devoid of respect for his own asceticism because it lacked outward display; 1.76.
While Jamadagni’s face was submerged up to his own knee-joints,
Viśvāmitra was terrified, Gālava’s throat was constricted, and Bhṛgu had sunk down.

With his gaze fixed upon the lotus-throne from which he had risen only a moment ago, his body rendered motionless by intense anger, and his limbs heavy with profound pride as if impaled on a spear before him.
Having perceived that he was seeking a seat, the four-faced god spoke with affection to his vehicle, the swan, as if smiling with the radiance of his own teeth blossoming forth.
"Sit upon my lap, my son, according to the most magnificent and wonderful rule;
for you are worthy of this, which accords with the honor arising from your multitude of virtues. (1.80)
Thus addressed by the Creator of the Universe, Dambha, though hesitant,
sat down with difficulty upon his lap after sprinkling it with a handful of water, free from apprehension.
Dambha said:

One must not speak loudly; if it is absolutely necessary to speak, one should cover the opening of the mouth with the lotus-hand so that I am not touched by the particles of breath from the mouth. (1.82)
Seeing his incomparable purity, Brahmā, with a smiling face,
shook the tip of his hand and said, "You are indeed hypocrisy."
Arise! Having descended upon the entire earth, which has the encircling moats of the oceans as its girdle, enjoy all pleasures—you who have not been truly recognized even by the gods. (1.84)
Thus dismissed by Brahmā with great reverence, he descended to the earth, binding the jewel of moral conduct around the necks of mortals who had fallen into the ocean of saṃsāra.
Then, having returned to the world of mortals and wandered through forests and cities, Dambha planted his banner of victory in the Gauḍa region and departed for the various quarters.

In speech there is the affectation of the Bāhlīkas; in religious vows and observances, that of the Easterners and Southerners; in authority, that of the heroes; and everywhere, the hypocrisy of the Gauḍas.
These companions of hypocrisy, by means of the powder perfected through the acceptance of gifts at a funeral feast,
apply a sectarian mark with ashes hither and thither in the morning.
Quickly dividing the beings upon the surface of the world into a thousand parts,
Hypocrisy dwells perpetually in embodied form within the mouths of the judges.

The heart of the preceptor is narrow-minded; the heart of the youth and the ascetic is [easily] penetrated; the heart of the official is crooked; the heart of one who has received initiation is [deceptive]; hypocrisy itself is the heart [of all these]. (1.90)
And thereafter, he took the hearts of the astrologers, physicians, servants, and merchants, along with the goldsmiths; and of the actors, soldiers, singers, reciters, and wandering mendicants.

Having entered the hearts of all living beings through various transformations by means of its parts, hypocrisy subsequently took possession of their inner selves, just as a bird enters the interior of trees with its wings.
Seeking fish, the crane-ascetic practices penance for a very long time, motionless on one leg at sacred bathing places; by this, hypocrisy has entered among the birds. (1.93)
That even trees— possessing abundant matted hair in the form of bark, emaciated by cold, heat, and wind, and constantly seeking water— are [thus], is also a manifestation of hypocrisy.
Thus should hypocrisy always be scrutinized as omnipresent within the hearts of all;
once it is known in its various forms, the illusion of deceivers becomes fruitless.
This deceptive transformation is a wish-fulfilling tree before the circle of deceivers;
in ancient times, the three worlds were traversed by Hari through the guise of a dwarf.
Canto 2:
Greed should always be contemplated; fear is seen on all sides from those who are greedy.
For one who is dragged away by greed, there is no discernment whatsoever between what ought to be done and what ought not to be done. (2.1)

Greed is a demon dwelling in a fortress of accumulated hoards; it is the destroyer of all, consisting of illusion, deception, delusion, denial, variety, fraud, and hypocrisy, and is the primary cause of all things. // 2.2 //

Lust, defeated by those who possess the wealth of goodness, who are tranquil through self-restraint and austerity, and who are learned in the scriptures, has entered the crooked hearts of merchants like a pit.

By means of fraudulent scales in buying and selling, light weights, secret embezzlement, and the protection of their own gains under false pretexts—these merchants, who are indeed thieves by day, joyfully plunder the people. (2.4)
Having spent the entire day stealing wealth from people through various fraudulent deceptions,
the merchant at home distributes with great difficulty only three cowrie shells.
One who is fond of tales always goes to listen to a holy book; bitten as it were by black snakes, he bears fruit through the practice of generosity and virtue. // 2.6 //

On the twelfth lunar day, on the anniversary of an ancestor’s death, during a solar or lunar transit, or at the eclipse of the moon or sun, he bathes for a very long time yet does not give away even a single cowrie shell. (2.7)
Casting his gaze in every direction, startled by the beggars, he draws his veil over his face and flees through the winding streets like a thief moving with crooked steps. (2.8)
At the time of sale, the deceitful merchant remains silent and gives no reply;
yet, upon seeing a man with a deposit in his hand, he engages in conversation. // 2.9 //
Seeing a man with hands empty of deposits, the merchant rises, bows, inquires after his welfare, offers him a seat, and engages him in a discourse on the Dharma. (2.10)
Someone says to him, having approached and deposited wealth [with him]: "Alas, brother, I shall depart tomorrow morning; today is a day of forced labor, what shall I do now? (2.11)
Having heard that, he spoke with wide-open eyes, feigning distress while acting falsely;
his eyes were fixed upon the task at hand as he looked repeatedly toward his side.
This place is under your control; however, guarding a trust for so long is difficult, and both time and place are unfavorable. Nevertheless, even so, I am your servant, O virtuous one.
"This auspicious [deposit], which ensures the safety of what is entrusted, is not defiled;
this has been repeatedly experienced by those who understand affairs—and you yourself know this. (2.14)
On an inauspicious day, something had previously been deposited by a certain friend; it was then quickly and gently brought back again in safety and well-being. (2.15)
Having thus secretly engaged in an improper discourse with the simple-minded one, the wicked man dances along with his various desires and seizes a heap of gold. (2.16)
With the infinite piles of profits from buying and selling produced by that grinding,
and with heaps of goods and counter-goods, he mocks the Lord of Wealth himself.
The treasure-pots of miserly merchants, though full, yield no enjoyment; they wither away like the breasts of young widows, which bear only the fruit of sorrow.
Deprived of both giving and enjoyment, they spend their time guarding gold;
these merchants are like great, venomous rats dwelling within the decaying mansion of saṃsāra and amidst the objects of the senses. (2.19)
Wandering with a terrifying display of his wildly whirling, broad garment, crooked and bristling with thorns, this serpent of fate is named the Lord of the City. // 2.20 //
Then that man, having wandered to the ends of the earth, by some stroke of fate,
returned after a very long time to his own country, destitute of wealth and devoid of companions.
Filled with apprehension, that merchant asks someone, "Where has that Great Being gone?
Approaching him, another says, "Friend, his splendor today is quite different. (2.22)
With various new silks, musk, sandalwood, camphor, black pepper, and betel nuts, he—chalk in hand—always counts millions in a mere moment. (2.23)
In this excellent palace, vast as Mount Meru and adorned with paintings upon its beautiful walls,
that great multitude dwells in happiness, for even the lord of the city follows after them.
Having heard this, his head reeling with incomparable astonishment, he went to that house and stood for a long time at the door, motionless and wearing a tattered rag.
But the merchant, having recognized him from within the lattice of the turret of his lofty palace,
could not draw breath, as if his mind were lost and his head struck by a thunderbolt.
Having approached very slowly and having somehow obtained an opportunity when no one else was present,
that man, manifesting his desire, begged him for his own wealth.
With a different look, knitting his brows and waving the tip of his hand, that wicked man of deceitful speech, whose livelihood was exhausted, said to him: "Where has this man come from? (2.28)
Who are you? To whom do you belong? Or from where? I do not even remember seeing you; what is the use of these words?
Alas! When, where, who are you? Tell me, what was given to whom, and by whom? (2.29)
Behold this misery! What kind of undesirable Kali age has arrived?
This world desires wealth from me, or perhaps it knows everything. (2.30)
In our lineage of Haragupta, even the taking of a deposit is impossible;
how much less the touch of a terrible great sin arising from denial? (2.31)
Furthermore, tell me, how can a person who constantly slanders others be accepted by the great?
Look for yourself at everything written on that day during the daytime.
"I am old and have laid down my burden upon my son; indeed, everything belonging to me is recorded in writing.
With his resolve thus destroyed by these words, he was dismissed and arrived at the presence of his son.
"The father knows it, the son knows it, and the father alone writes it all"—thus for him there is a long cycle of coming and going, like that of a ball. (2.34)
When he has reached the gate of the royal palace and has received the reward for his exile,
the merchant endures the king’s wrath but does not surrender even a fraction of the coin.
Though tormented by the king with various instruments of torture,
he simply says, "There is nothing at all placed in my hand."
Thus, those greedy for their own nature possess an intense thirst for the salt water of wealth;
they would cast away their own bodies like a blade of grass, yet not even a fraction of their riches. (2.37)
In former times, Śukra, desiring wealth, approached his childhood friend Vaiśravaṇa, the lord of riches and the deity who is the abode of all prosperity, and spoke to him.
"O friend, this abundance of yours, which surpasses the sovereignty of gods and asuras, brings supreme joy to your friends and sorrow to your enemies. (2.39)
While you are my well-wishing friend and lord of wealth, I am destitute yet burdened with a large family;
for they praise as a true friend one who shares equally in sorrow and joy and who acts out of his own free will.
The fortunes of the great—those who show honor toward fame, whose wealth is enjoyed by supplicants, and who are born of noble lineages—are for the enjoyment of their friends. (2.41)
That which has been brought near by those with vast stores of merit—preserved with effort—is a refuge in prosperity and in adversity, and serves as both a treasure and a friend. (2.42)
Thus addressed with confidence by the preceptor of the Daityas in that secluded place, the Giver of Wealth (Kubera),
constrained by both affection and greed, reflected for a long time and spoke to him.
Knowing you to be my childhood friend, in whom I have cultivated extreme affection, yet I am not able to abandon this fragment of wealth which is the very life of my life. (2.44)
Relatives become friends through many shared tasks when seeking affection;
wives and sons are easily obtained, but wealth alone is difficult to find in this world.
The giving of wealth is exceedingly rash, extremely difficult, and most wonderful;
for while some give even their bodies, they do not give away even a fraction of their riches.
Thus rejected by the Lord of Wealth with the dismissal of his hopes,
Śukra departed with a dejected face, a distracted mind, and a countenance flushed with shame.
Having deliberated for a long time at home with his ministers, that great yogin entered the heart of the Lord of Wealth by means of his illusory power (*māyā*) in order to seize all his riches.
Vaiśravaṇa, whose body was indeed possessed by Śukra and who was capable of relinquishing everything,
bestowed wealth upon the twice-born according to the signals given by him.
When the preceptor of the Dānavas had departed after seizing all of Kubera’s wealth,
the Lord of Wealth, realizing it was an illusion, grieved for a long time.
Placing his hand upon his forehead, he reflected along with Śaṅkha, Mukunda, Padma, and the others on the transformation of semen; then, sighing hotly, he spoke.
I have been deceived by Śukra, a friend who knows my vital secrets, a deceitful and excessively greedy rogue, who is difficult to overcome due to his reliance on the Daityas. // 2.52 //
Now, destitute of wealth, having in an instant attained the lightness of a blade of grass, to whom shall I tell my sorrow? What shall I do, or where shall I go? (2.53)
People abandon one who is destitute of wealth; one who is destitute of people encounters insults.
For one who is insulted, the transformation brought by calamity upon the body is a great burden.
Alas! When beloved wealth and life itself have departed—those very things which are like watering-basins for the creeper of dharma for those who possess a body—everything goes with them.

One who possesses wealth becomes learned, fortunate, respected, renowned for his deeds, of noble lineage, and heroic; yet one devoid of wealth, though endowed with all virtues, is considered devoid of merit. (2.56)
Thus, his heart withered by the fire of the unbearable affliction of separation from his wealth,
Dhanapa reflected for a long time with his ministers and went for refuge to the god Śarva.
Maheśvara, the refuge of the universe, who had previously become his friend,
was informed of his own situation by him and dispatched a messenger to Śukra.

The Conqueror of the Cities spoke to Śukra, who had arrived suddenly summoned by the messengers, whose brilliance was as bright as the light of wealth, and who stood before him with his hands joined in a gesture of reverence like a crown.
Alas, the Lord of Wealth has been deceived by you, who are grateful; for even a person who is ungrateful does not, indeed, proceed to commit treachery against a friend.
That deception which is practiced by one of unreckonable fame who has abandoned his station and is ungrateful—
such deception is not fitting toward you, who are a kind, affectionate, and passionate friend.
O wise one, was this deed—which you have performed and which suppresses the arising of virtue—consistent with what you have heard, suitable for your vow, or in accordance with your lineage? (2.62)
Was this the practice of good conduct, or tranquility, or the instruction of your elders, or the innate power of your intellect, by which you have come to such deception? (2.63)
To whom is wealth not dear? Whose mind is not captivated by wealth?
Yet those greedy for the riches of fame do not seek their goals through evil deeds.
Do not, O do not defile the stainless and pure lineage of Bhṛgu with the stain of greed;
for greed is a cloud to the royal swans of spotless fame.
Having abandoned infinite fame for the sake of objects that are like blades of grass tossed by the wind, what kind of rogue is he who accepts them in the midst of rogues? (2.66)
He who, with a crooked mind, deceives another by abandoning virtuous conduct, is himself the one deceived, for he has cheated his own self, which is the source of all merit. 2.67.

Alas, for those whose fame has been sullied, their fortune—though naturally as tender as a young sprout—is inevitably rendered senseless by the fragrances arising from the poisonous trees of slander. (2.68)
For indeed, the stainless crystal mirror of the pure fame of virtuous people does not become tarnished by the sighs of a populace distressed by humiliation. (2.69)
This action, improper and exceedingly defiled, has manifested from delusion; let its purification be accomplished simply by the restoration of another's wealth. (2.70)
Wipe with your own hand your stainless fame, which has been soiled by the dust of slander;
follow our words and relinquish this wealth belonging to another.
Thus addressed with conciliatory words by the God of gods, the teacher of the three worlds,
Śukra— whose thirst was bound to the wealth of others— spoke with palms joined in reverence.

O Blessed One, who indeed would out of delusion transgress your teaching, which rests upon the tips of the crowns of the lords of the gods, were it not for the misfortune that carries away living beings? (2.73)
When one's wealth is exhausted, and the servants, wife, and sons suffer in the house, who would have any consideration for what ought and ought not to be done regarding the giving of money? (2.74)
I have constantly reflected that the Lord of Wealth, consisting of my friend, would be my protection in times of calamity;
and now he has grown exceedingly great, becoming a firm bond of hope within my heart.
Having approached and entreated me, this man, casting aside shame and himself devoid of modesty, suddenly severed my hope with the weapon of refusal. (2.76)
By him, through delusion, was wrought a weaponless slaughter, a fireless burning, and a death devoid of poison; for by that rogue, the shattering of hope was inflicted.
Therefore, this enemy of mine is equal to a virtuous deed; for wealth acquired through deceit, even if blameless, is a sin that deceives one's enemies when one is empty-handed. (2.78)
"Not even a tiny bit of wealth should be surrendered by you when I have made it known as the truth; for wealth is life itself, and the loss of wealth is the loss of life. (2.79)
Thus, as the preceptor of the Daityas spoke repeatedly and entreated him many times over,
Virūpākṣa suddenly devoured him in a rage of refusal.
Within the belly of the Destroyer of Cities, his body being boiled in the vast and terrifying expanse of the fire of universal destruction, Śukra cried out with lamentation.
Urged again and again with the harsh words, "Renounce wealth," Śukra replied:
"O Blessed One, let death be my lot; I will not renounce even the slightest bit of wealth."
Then Śukra, having fallen into the belly of Hara— which was terrifying with thousands of flames of fire intensified by his *dhāraṇā* and profoundly deep— cried out piteously.
The God of gods said to him: "O you who are consumed by a wicked obsession, abandon the wealth of others;
do not go to your destruction in this submarine fire within the great ocean of the belly."

He said: "In this world, death in a fire thick with streams of marrow and bone-marrow bursting forth from excessive heat is better; I shall not give up even a single particle of wealth while I still breathe. (2.85)
Furthermore, Śukra, his life reduced to a mere fraction of a moment, set ablaze by the fire of the dhāraṇī of the most terrible, rising fire of Time, offered a hymn of praise to the Goddess.
When Rudra had been propitiated by Gaurī through her hymn of praise and was moved by affection,
Śukra regained his composure at her word and emerged through the opening of his seminal duct.
Thus, those greedy for their own nature endure even the most intense torment; yet they do not relinquish their wealth, just as a base person does not abandon innate crookedness.
Therefore, deceitful artifice arising from greed, crooked in its course, is illusion;
it dwells within those whose hearts are greedy, for one who is not greedy does not practice deception. (2.89)
Desire, through its loveliness, produces an inexplicable and intense delusion; like poison, it suddenly snatches away life with its deceptive sweetness. 3.1
For these elephants, agitated by passion, are quickly bound by women who have their rut indicated by the humming of swarms of bees clinging to their fragrance. (3.2)
Does not the lordly elephant, robbed of his senses by passion and deceived by desire, endure kicks from feet, the striking of cold goads, and confinement in fetters and the like? (3.3)
Restrained by long-standing calamities, knowing how to knit his brows yet fallen into subjection, a man helpless before sense-objects is made to dance by women like a peacock in play. (3.4)
Women, intent on attracting the blood [of men] through their illusions during the nights of the darkness of delusion, steal away the hearts of the simple-minded like female goblins. (3.5)
One who falls under their power is never released from women—who are snares for the deer of passion, a multitude of chains for binding the elephant of the heart, and fresh creepers of calamity. (3.6)

He who, having conquered his own self, understands the illusory magic of cyclic existence, the magic of Śambara, and the magic of mental distraction—even he does not understand the illusion of women. (3.7)
Whose mind do women—who possess bodies as delicate as flowers yet whose true nature is as hard as diamond-stone, and whose conduct is so varied—not bewilder within? (3.8)

Women who are alienated from those who love them, who are humble yet arrogant, who are passionate toward those who are detached, who are intent on deceptive speech, and who harbor doubts regarding true sincerity. (3.9)

He alone is truly born in this world whose wife—her limbs curved with coquettish grace, seen by many people, and a banner signaling the destruction of one's fortitude—is not the mistress in his house. (3.10)
When a husband has been conquered by the transformations of intoxication and rendered mute and senseless by women, the entire layer of dust from the house is thrown into his face. (3.11)
With her amorous arts rendered indistinct by her efforts, appearing as if naturally innocent,
she asks her bold husband for a moon-disc to serve as a forehead mark.
Exhausted by her own wandering to and fro, the husband of that fickle woman, conquered by her charms, massages her feet under the pretext of visiting sacred bathing places.

With one [man] she delights him with a change in her eyes, with another with her words, with another with her gestures, and with yet another with sexual union; by her very nature, a woman assumes many forms.

To whom does this woman belong—she who is a *payaicapa* (water-bird) yet a fickle *kurāṅgī* (deer), a *bhṛṅgī* (bee) on another's tree yet a *mātaṅgī* (elephant) by nature, a *bhṛṅgī* (bee) bearing false delusions, and a *bhujaṅgī* (female serpent) who is crooked? 3.15.
"In private, women always say with a sigh of relief: 'Blessed is the courtesan who enjoys the wealth for the sake of manifold, unrestrained, and youthful sexual pleasures. (3.16)
Fickle, she stays upon the palace roof, singing as she gazes down at the street; she runs about without cause, her laughter wild like a string of crystal stones.
"My husband knows nothing at all of how to speak or act; he is like a beast," having said this, the woman manages the male affairs within her own household.
She rises to greet him with the coming and going of his business, she goes out herself, and she speaks loudly at home—such is the wife of one who is dead while still living. (3.19)
The wife of a jealous elder, the wife of a servant, or the wife of an official; the woman of an artisan or a man of ill-repute, the wife of a hunter, or the wife of a merchant-leader. (3.20)

She was by nature fond of socializing with young people and affectionate toward them; she was intent on enumerating the multitude of virtues in others, yet constantly spoke of the faults of her own husband. (3.21)
A woman with little wealth but great enjoyment; one who is beautiful yet has an ugly wife; or a charming young bride, skilled in all arts, distressed by association with the base. (3.22)
Addicted to gambling and drinking wine, fond of long stories and songs, skilled [in these arts], with many unchaste women as her companions, she was naturally partial toward brave men. (3.23)
Having abandoned domestic affairs, assuming many kinds of disguises, practicing without restraint, possessing ready wit for retorts, devoid of truth, and inherently shameless— (3.24)
Devoted to inquiries after the news of health and virtue, her speech was charming with expressions of affection;
she delighted in various diversions in secluded places and was openly devoted to the goddess Sāvitrī.
Devoted to visiting sacrificial sites, temples, astrologers, physicians, and the homes of kinsmen;
she indulges in feasting, drinking, lavish expenditures, expeditions, and festivals as if she were independent. (3.26)

Devoted to monks and ascetics, detached from her own kin, attached to what is pleasing to the mind, devoted to the initiation of [spiritual] vision, detached from her beloved, and endowed with meditative concentration. // 3.27 //
She who delights in social gatherings and friends should be known as one whose conduct is ruined. (A Kulaka) // 3.28 //

Constantly attached to faults, they delude the people; possessed by many planetary influences, they are fickle. Like female demons at twilight, these cruel women seize away the glow of passion. (3.29)

To whom is he not worthy of being borne? To those of deluded intellect who are intent on trivial pursuits, and to those unrestrained men who, out of passion, delight in the tranquility of peace yet remain attached to fickle women.
The display of passion and valor, and the description of their various improper gifts—this alone is their incantation and mechanical device for subjugation. (3.31)
Whose heart does not tremble at the cruel conduct of women, who possess a thousand illusions that roam like night-stalkers through the darkness of the Kali age? (3.32)

In former times, there was a lord of merchants renowned throughout the earth named Dhanadatta; having surpassed the wealth of the Lord of Wealth (Kubera), he was like the ocean, a repository for jewels. (3.33)

To him was born a daughter named Vasumatī, whose limbs were exquisitely beautiful like the embodied form of the god of love, and who had conquered the quarters with the playful glances of her eyes. (3.34)
Being childless, he gave that beloved daughter, whom he had treated as a son,
to the merchant Samudradatta, whose wealth and noble lineage were equal to his own.
Delighting with that fawn-eyed woman for a long time in his father-in-law’s house,
he once set out ahead of a caravan that had arrived from an island.
When her husband had departed for his father’s house, that young woman ascended to the roof-terrace of the palace and sported with her friends,
who were restless in their playful dalliance.
On the palace roof, that large-eyed woman saw on the road a man whose form was like that of the God of Love;
at the mere sight of him, her composure vanished somewhere, as if overcome by a corrupted mind.
Suddenly robbed by him as if by a thief, that woman of tremulous eyes lost her power of discernment and became utterly unable to restrain the transformations of love.
"O fickle one, do not let your virtue fall like a river into the bed of its own family!"—
thus it was as if her girdle, noisy and agitated by trembling, cried out loudly for a long time.
Having engaged in conversation with him in private, she brought that young man;
for who is able to restrain a lover once he has been set in motion? (3.41)
That wanton woman delighted with him through the blossoming of desires, the playful charms of love-making, delightful jests and laughter, and their abiding in natural affection. (3.42)
Then, having completed his own business at home and being eager to behold his beloved, Samudradatta, with great haste and grand preparations, entered his father-in-law’s residence.
Having passed the day with his beloved amidst a multitude of enjoyments and riches, while the people were preoccupied with the play of a vast and great festival, he went to his bedchamber.

In a delightful place where a most excellent bed had been prepared, a canopy was fixed, the fragrance of incense wafted abroad, and it resembled a celestial palace with its blazing jewel-lamps. // 3.45 //

There, having embraced his beloved whose lotus-eyes were tremulous with the intoxication of honeyed wine, he, longing for pleasure, reclined upon the couch like a rutting elephant beside a fresh lotus pond.
She too, her gaze fixed solely upon the meditation of the Supreme Being dwelling within her heart, remained for a long time with eyes closed, absorbed in contemplation like a female yoginī.
During the embraces, kisses, and the loosening of her girdle, she— breathing heavily and with limbs drawn together against her husband— remembered only that thief of her virtue.
Thinking that she was angry out of affection, Samudradatta, her simple-minded husband,
prostrated himself and entreated her with flattering words for the sake of her favor.
Stupid beasts among men, utterly deluded, take excessive pleasure in women who are impassioned by other men, who turn their faces away, and who are perverse in their love and desire. (3.50)
What can be done? This desire is directed toward another, yet it is a desire for independence;
for even at twilight, when she is enamored with hundreds of riches, the sun remains full of passion.
Having long reflected upon her lover who had been placed by appointment in a hidden grove of trees, she regarded her own husband as if he were poison and fell into a swoon.
When Samudradatta’s eyes were sealed by sleep and he was exhausted from his affectionate attentions,
she rose, adjusted her attire, and stood quietly, intent on departing.
At that very moment, the thief entered that house while the people were dazed and intoxicated;
remaining unobserved, he saw her, adorned with jingling ornaments, eager to depart.
In the meantime, the moon, as if startled, quickly trembled while closely embracing the quarter of the sky beloved to the king of the gods, which was almost entirely closed up.
The moonlight spread forth like the feigned smile of the night, which was closing its lotuses while shining with the blossoming of water-lilies.
Seeing the heavens weary from the heat of the sun yet gladdened by the rising moon,
the ponds— laden with swarms of bees and the fragrance of night-lotuses— seemed, as it were, to laugh through their clusters of *kumuda* flowers.

The Night, having cast off her veil of darkness stolen away by the rays of the moon, took up before her a garment consisting of swarms of bees agitated by the fragrance of night-lotuses, as if overcome with shame.
Then, at the middle of the night when the people were asleep and the moonlight had spread wide,
she proceeded slowly toward the grove, as if in the darkness and free from all apprehension.
Then, consumed by the god of uneven arrows, she entered her own garden garden helpless;
she was followed by a thief who had been astonished by her ornaments and followed her out of greed for them.
There he beheld his beloved, adorned with radiant and lovely garments and shimmering flowers; appearing in the forest as a source of apprehension, he was nevertheless recognized by the birds.
He was scorched by the mass of flames from the fire of separation from his beloved heart,
and burned by the rays of the moon, which, though its light shone upon the face of the quarters, acted as a fire with its beams.
Having abandoned all hope due to the long duration of their secret tryst, he let his life-breath depart by clinging to a circle of creepers entwined upon a tree, awaiting a reunion with his beloved.
Upon seeing him, she melted away, lamenting amidst calamity, grief, and terror;
the slender woman fell like a creeper, agitated by the circling of humming bees.
Her eyes closed in a swoon, she remained for a long time embracing the earth; then, slowly regaining her breath, she lamented at will with low-voiced sobs.
Alas, alas! O delight of my eyes, where indeed is that face of yours, beautiful as the clear moon?
Of little merit as I am, when shall I behold it? What is this? Where am I, and where is my beloved? (3.66)
Thus, having lamented with fresh compassion and having carefully released the noose, the weak woman took him in her arms and kissed his face, as if infusing life back into him.
Enchanted, she placed his lotus-face upon her own mouth and filled it with betel, as if manifesting her passion through her outward form.
Then, summoned by the fragrance of her heaps of flowers, musk, incense, and other perfumes,
a vetāla entered the corpse’s body and cut off her nose.
Having reaped the fruit of misconduct appropriate to her fickleness, she went with her nose cut off, entered the house, and cried out loudly to her husband, "Alas! Alas! (3.70).
When all the people were held in check and Samudradatta was no longer afraid, she wailed, "This is my nose that has been cut off by my husband! (3.71)
Questioned by his circle of kinsmen, including his father-in-law and others, who were all enraged, Samudradatta, though sold in a foreign land, said nothing at all, like one who is mute. (3.72)
Then, when his kinsmen announced this at the king's assembly at the break of day,
the king’s wrath fell upon Samudradatta, and there was a heavy fine of wealth imposed upon him.
The thief, too, having witnessed the entire event with his own eyes, was filled with wonder;
he reported it before the king and received honors such as a portion of the kingdom and other rewards.
In the garden Śavavadana, having shown him her nose,
she performed for Samudradatta a purification that befitted a disinterested friend.
Thus, he who understands that these women are exceedingly crooked, of cruel conduct, shameless, and fickle—he, the wise man, is never deceived by them. (3.76)
There too, the courtesans are exceedingly crooked, deceiving the world with feigned passion; by their deceitful conduct, even Vaiśravaṇa himself would become a mendicant. (4.1)
Captivating, most restless, and possessing many waves, the sixty-four arts flow downward like rivers; they are within the heart of a courtesan just as [rivers] are within the ocean. (4.2)

The art of dress, the art of dance, the art of song, the art of sidelong glances, the art of knowing the ways of love, the art of seizing [the opportunity], and the art of deceiving friends. // 4.3 //

The art of drinking, the art of play, the art of sexual union, the art of the intervals between embraces, the art of kissing, the art of passion for another, and the art of shameless impetuosity and agitation. // 4.4 //

The art of jealousy and playful quarreling, the art of weeping, the art of destroying pride, the art of perspiration, dizziness, and trembling, and furthermore, the art of exclusive adornment. // 4.5 //

The state of being motionless and unable to close her eyes; the state resembling one who is dead; the state of passion that cannot endure separation; and the state of resolve to reject his anger. // 4.6 //

The art of quarreling with his own mother, the art of observing the festival of entering a virtuous household, the art of abduction, the art of his birth, the art of play, and the art of the king of thieves. // 4.7 //

The art of slackening respect, the art of speaking faults without cause, the art of piercing with pain, the art of anointing [the body], and the arts of sleep, the eyes, and wearing soiled garments. // 4.8 //
The art of harshness, the art of sharpness, the art of seizing by the throat and applying a bolt, and the art of rejecting the sight, touch, journey, and praise of a lover. // 4.9 //
The arts of sporting at sacred fords, in groves, and in the abodes of the gods; the art of household management;
the arts of subjugating through herbs and mantras; the art of arboriculture; and the art of dyeing the hair. // 4.10 //

Having exhausted sixty-three arts—including the various meritorious arts of mendicancy and asceticism, as well as the art of visiting the islands—at the end, she became a courtesan through the art of the procuress. 4.11.
Even for her who surrenders herself through a portion of her wealth to those whose names and castes are unknown, those of vain resolve still seek to investigate her true nature. (4.12)

A certain person—either naked or destitute, yet broken by a multitude of virtues—consumes the tainted wealth acquired through the deception of all people by those whose hearts are consumed by passion. (4.13)
Even a low-born horseman, an elephant driver, or a most wicked artisan becomes the beloved of those women who have deceived all people. (4.14)
King Vikramasiṃha, having been previously defeated by powerful monarchs,
departed for Vidarbha out of pride, accompanied by his minister Guṇayaśas.
There, having entered the house of a courtesan, he visited the world-renowned Vilāsavatī, a prostitute who was enjoyed by men of great wealth, even though he himself possessed little means. (4.16)
Beholding that being of vast strength, who was enjoying vessels worthy of royal insignia,
she made her various treasuries of jewels and gold dependent upon his expenditure.
Observing her spontaneous and unswerving devotion and propriety, the king,
overcome with wonder, spoke of her great magnanimity out of love in a secluded place.
It is strange that even this courtesan squanders so much wealth for my sake as if it were a blade of grass;
for the affection of courtesans is based on money and is cast aside once the path of pleasure has been traversed.
Prostitutes display affection out of greed for even a tiny fragment of wealth; yet she who squanders even that wealth—what doubt can there be regarding her love? (4.20)
Having heard these words of the lord of the earth, he laughed and, with resentment, said to him: "O King, who can have confidence in the conduct of a courtesan? (4.21)
Devoid of truth, clinging to fragments of wealth, and dependent on fleeting moments of pleasure—these courtesans, sweet as honey to the face, enter the hearts of those who lack discernment. (4.22)
Both hopes and courtesans grant the pleasure of the first encounter, cause distress and exile in the middle, and yield the fruit of suffering for men in the end. (4.23)
Even today, they have not been understood in their true nature even by the immortals such as Hari and Hara;
for both courtesans and the illusions of saṃsāra are full of delusion, confusion, and great infatuation. (4.24)
Having heard these words of his minister and having reached an agreement with him, the king made himself out to be falsely dead in order to test the courtesan.
When that corpse had been placed upon the fire of the practitioner’s mind by the mantra-master, Vilāsavatī, adorned as she was, suddenly ascended to the realm of fire.
Embracing her with both arms as she was struck by the violent force of the falling, fiercely blazing, and radiant flames, the king joyfully cried out, "I live! (4.27)
Reflecting upon her firm and true love,
the king, his affection aroused, repeatedly censured the minister who was intent upon the qualities of a courtesan.
Then the lord of the earth, taking for himself the vast accumulation of the courtesan’s wealth which was at his disposal, assembled an army formidable with elephants, horses, and warriors.
Having conquered the lords of the earth with the vast floods of forces he had amassed, that protector of the world returned to his own realm, bringing joy like the full moon.
And that slender Vilāsavatī, having been placed upon the heads of the beauties of the inner apartments by the king,
shone like the goddess Śrī, her tresses disheveled by the breeze of the yak-tail fans.
Then once, having bowed with palms joined in reverence, she spoke to the lord in private: "O Lord, I, your maidservant, have long served you as if you were a wish-fulfilling tree."
O Lord, if indeed I have anywhere become the cause of your prosperity,
you ought, by your grace, to make my hope fruitful.
For the meeting of great men— who have attained the fruits of merit, who have removed the dust of others, and whose nature is pure— is indeed never fruitless, just like that of sacred fords.
I had a certain beloved youth, a suitor dearer to me than wealth or life;
by the power of fate, he was imprisoned in the city of Vidarbha in the guise of a thief.
To liberate him, I have served you, O Lord of the Earth, as one most capable; now let that which is fitting for your courage, your lineage, and your heroism be performed.
Having heard these words, the king, as if struck by deception and filled with wonder,
gazed at the earth for a very long time and recalled the minister's speech.
Then, having consoled her in that very manner and having conquered the king of Vidarbha,
he brought about a reunion for her with her thief, who was released from his bonds.
Thus, with many hearts, many tongues, many hands, and many deceptions—devoid of truth in reality—who clearly knows courtesans? (4.39)

One courtesan is beloved for her beauty; another is beloved for her wealth; yet another is beloved for her service as a slave; another is beloved for protection; and still another is beloved for her jesting. (4.40)
Canto 5:
Delusion, which seizes all people, first robs them of their very intellect; it dwells most secretly within the mouths of scribes and in their writings. (5.1)
The abundant harvest, like the full digit of the fierce Raudrī,
was seen to be devoured in an instant, leaving nothing behind, like the digit of the moon swallowed by the eclipse-demon Rāhu.
The arts of cyclic existence are known by yogis who have abandoned passion and delusion;
but the arts of the scribe are not known by anyone, even with great effort. (5.3)

The entire population was devoured not by Time, but by scribes alone— with their hundreds of camps for fraudulent arts, their hiding places for wealth and grain, and their darkness like the night of universal destruction.
For these are the men of Time, who strike down the world with the fall of their exceedingly broad staffs;
they wander through the world like Piśācas of calculation, bearing birch-bark banners marked with numbers.
One should place no trust in those whose horns are as crooked as the tips of Yama’s buffalo-horns, and upon whose neck the noose of the Destroyer is not yet fastened. (5.6)
Under the guise of ink-drops emerging from the tip of the pen, the Goddess of Royal Fortune, being scratched by the scribe's stylus, weeps with tear-drops mixed with collyrium as if she were weary.
Who in this world has not been deluded by the scribes, who employ uneven finger-marks and whose rows of hair-like curls are as crooked as those of illusory women? (5.8)
The world is constantly destroyed by the senses residing in the body, which devour the multitude of sense-objects and deceive all beings with the accumulation of the manifold play of illusion.
The curved arrangements of the letters appear like the snares of Death; upon the surface of the birch-bark scroll held by the scribe, they resemble serpents coiled within a circle.
For these Citraguptas— of variegated intellects, secret-seizers, and scribes—
are those who, by destroying even a single stroke of the pen, turn what is consistent into something inconsistent.
In this world, only very minor arts are well known among scribes;
indeed, it is Kali or the God of Death who knows their secret arts.
The art of the arrangement of the curved script, the art of closing all the limbs, the art of constant entry, collection, and concealment, and the art of increasing expenditure. // 5.13 //
The art of seizing property, the art of taking wealth through extortion, the art of plundering by means of bribes, and the art of fleeing to the borderlands. // 5.14 //
The art of discerning what remains, the art of devouring an entire moving mass, the art of concealing what has arisen, and the art of displaying what is lost or shattered. // 5.15 //

The art of supporting oneself through trade, the art of decline through long journeys and such, both combined in one place on the fifteenth day, along with the arts of thievery, medicine, and sitting in council. // 5.16 //

And at the end, from the complete burning of the birch-bark, there is the destruction of the arrival [of the record], without which the legal practitioner would be left in darkness when grasping the documents. (5.17)
These sixteen crooked digits of the scribe—who is stained with blemish, subject to decay, possessing ever-new forms, and increasing—are mines of faults. 5.18.

Those who are firm and established in their station, by means of the perfected mantra in every way, instantly effect the cutting off of the cycle of illusion, just as teachers do for one who has understood it. // 5.19 //
In former times, a gambler whose wealth, cattle, and clothing had been lost, abandoned by his kinsmen out of fear of theft, wandered the entire earth in the grip of intense misfortune. (5.20)
Once, having come to Ujjayinī by virtue of his merits, he bathed there and,
while wandering through the deserted city, beheld the temple of Śiva.
Having gone to the empty abode, he, free from worldly activity, constantly served the boon-granting god Mahākāla with ointments, flowers, and fruits. (5.22)
There he remained for a very long time, sleepless through the nights with hymns, recitations, songs, lamps, and profound meditations, for the sake of destroying unbearable misery.
Once, having been suddenly propitiated by his devotion produced through a hundred auspicious deeds,
the Blessed Lord, the Master of Beings who removes the fear of worldly existence, spoke to him.
When the God said, "Son, take one," he repeatedly made a sign to the Enemy of Pura regarding a single skull at the summit of his garland of skulls.
When half-spoken, Rudra silenced himself with a sign of pressure from his skull-cup, remaining mute due to the poverty of the merits of gamblers.
When he had gone to bathe in that secluded place, the God spoke to him, displaying before him his skull as if it were the Ganges with its fringe of rays from a mass of teeth.
"Why have you, in granting a boon to this honest gambler who has been your devotee for so long, caused me to lose consciousness with such torments? (5.28)

When the Blessed One had thus questioned the skull, it spoke slowly with a smile: "I live by the drops of nectar from the moon upon my crest, which fall as they are melted by the heat of the Three-Eyed God's eye. (5.29)
Listen, O Blessed One, whose nature is straightforward: by whom have you been petitioned? For who could possibly instruct even an easily accessible Lord without a motive? (5.30)
This gambler, exceedingly miserable and having abandoned all his own duties due to poverty,
prepares plaster, offerings, flowers, incense, and water-libations in this palace.
The ascetic becomes sorrowful and destitute of wealth; yet he remains devoted to the Dharma. Having fallen from his office and prosperity, he becomes humble toward all and speaks kindly. (5.32)
A man without wealth honors gods and brahmins, mutters prayers for a long time, and knows his friend;
even a hard lump of iron becomes workable when heated. (5.33)
Everyone whose heart is tormented by calamity remains steadfast in right conduct;
what need is there to speak of the recollection of past deeds for those deluded by the intoxication of wealth?

O Blessed One, one who desires sovereignty and wealth, being suspended by the snare of hope, performs supreme worship; yet once that object has been attained, he is no longer seen [engaged in such devotion]. (5.35)
Those who strive for their own ends, having already attained their goals, are always fruitless as servants;
for indeed, there is no one in this world who, having completed his task, remains a servant.

"O King, when this palace has been filled with the full array of enjoyments such as fruits, water, and flowers, once the gambler has departed and it is left desolate, no others will maintain it. (5.37)
Therefore, O Blessed One, always protect this gambler who has come to you through his merit; for him to grant a boon would be the banishment of your own worship.
Having heard these most artful words, the wielder of the Pināka bow, smiling with great wonder, asked him: "Who are you in truth, and what is your deed? (5.39)
Thus questioned, Kapāla immediately reflected upon the true state of affairs and replied: "I was born among the Magadhas in a family of scribes, but I turned my back on my own worldly duties. (5.40)
Devoted to ritual bathing, recitation, and vows, intent upon sacred fords, and having understood the meaning of all the scriptures,
he cast off his body in the Bhāgīrathī and attained your state.
Having heard this, the Blessed One said: "Kāyastha, it is true that you are such;
it is a marvel that even though you are reduced to a mere skull, you do not abandon the art of crookedness."
Having spoken thus, making the creepers of the quarters white with flowers by means of the rays of his smile,
the Giver of Boons granted a boon to that gambler who had returned after bathing.
While he was looking on, the moon-crested Lord quickly performed that deed intended by the gambler and extracted his head from the row of the finest severed heads upon his garland.
Thus, even when reduced to mere bones, the scribe does not relinquish his innate, crooked, and foul art, which is intent on the destruction of people— like the fang of Yama.

What person indeed could remain healthy by relying upon those things situated within the body—which are defiled by their constant state of impurity and produce faults—any more than one would rely upon excrement? (5.46)
By that wise man who, through diligent effort, discovered the deception of the scribe devised by the Asuras, let this jewel-filled earth be well protected.
Chapter 6: A Description of Pride.
Pride alone is the enemy that has taken up residence in the hearts of all people;
possessed by it, one becomes paralyzed, neither hearing nor seeing. (6.1)

That which was known as self-restraint among people who had conquered their own selves in the Kṛta age, that very same thing exists in the Kali age among men in the form of its opposite: intoxication.
Silence, the contraction of the mouth, upward-looking eyes, a lack of attention to others,
and the smearing and binding of the limbs— this is the foremost form of intoxication.
The intoxication of valor, the intoxication of beauty, the intoxication of passion, and the intoxication of noble lineage—
these trees of intoxication, born from the root of the intoxication of wealth, end in ruin for embodied beings.
The wind-like [feeling] is like being impaled on a stake; the stiffness is like that of a corpse; the pride of wealth amidst great enjoyments is like a feverish complication of the humors. (6.5)
One who displays his arms is intoxicated by valor; one who looks into a mirror and the like is intoxicated by beauty;
one who gazes upon women is intoxicated by passion; but this man, blind from birth, is intoxicated by wealth.
With eyes closed in a swoon from the essence of inner bliss, absorbed in concentrated meditation—
this intoxication with wealth among men is something like the delight of one who finds pleasure in the Self.
This other [type of] intoxication, devoid of all virtues, characterized by various distortions and directed toward no object, is a strange and supportless delusion that triumphs. (6.8)
One who gazes at the sky does not see the ground because of his pillar-like rigidity; one intoxicated by asceticism is always proud;
one intoxicated by devotion performs wonders; and one who has forgotten his body is fickle by his very nature. (6.9)

With eyes reddened by agitation, unable to endure even the mere words of others, and prone to incoherent ravings—he is the unevenness of passion incarnate, a physical disturbance of the humors in men. // 6.10 //
Fierce with a constant frown, harsh in his abuse, intent on violent assault,
intoxicated by power, devouring everything— such is the cruel rākṣasa among men.
Forgetting all other personal duties due to the stories of the prowess of his ancestors, pride of lineage alone is the man’s far-sighted and great wisdom. (6.12)
Having abandoned all tactile contact, free from support through the contemplation of universal impurity, he is as if smeared even in space; prideful of his purity, he is in constant contraction.
All intoxications, being fraught with danger, perish when their respective roots are destroyed;
yet the one crooked pride of the serpent-like enjoyer alone expands boundlessly.
But intoxication from drink is the lowest of all, a source of universal loathing and a state of great delusion;
though it lasts but a moment, it suddenly destroys the virtue accumulated over a thousand years. (6.15)

Whether toward a learned and eminent brahmin, a cow, an elephant, a king, or even an outcaste, one who is intoxicated by liquor views them with equanimity and does not perceive the distinction between self and other. (6.16)
One whose distinction between the real and the unreal has dissolved, who views gold, clods of earth, and stones as equal,
and who has attained even the state of a yogi— such a person, if intoxicated, falls into hell by his own accord.
He weeps, sings, laughs, sings, laments, and falls into deep delusion;
intoxicated by the mirror-disk of the world, he undergoes manifold transformations. (6.18)
Does one who is intoxicated not feel distress upon seeing his beloved intent on kissing another?
Having drunk honey with intense passion, does he become free from passion? (6.19)
The intoxicated man casts his garment far away and takes up unbearable calamity;
he drinks from the hollow of his cupped hands the moon manifested as his own urine.
In the past, the great seer Cyavana, having obtained youth through the application of the Aśvins,
being grateful himself, made them both worthy of drinking the Soma at his sacrifice.
Enraged, Śakra approached him and said: "O sage, do you not know anything?
The two Aśvins are physicians; they are unworthy of the company of the assembly, yet they are worthy of the Soma."
Thus, although repeatedly forbidden by the Lord of the Gods, Cyavana— firm of resolve through his own splendor—
did not waver from his duty out of affection for the Aśvins.
The Lord of Sages, a vessel for the manifestation of his majestic power, paralyzed the long, pillar-like arm of Jambhāri, which was raised with its vajra ready for that wrath.
And for his destruction, he created a terrible great Asura in the form of a magical apparition, possessing a body like that of Pralamba, with four tusks, and a vastness of a thousand yojanas.
Possessed by him, the wielder of the thunderbolt was suddenly terrified and fled to him for refuge;
with his fortitude lost, he said, "Let Soma be the physician for the two gods."
The Sage too, an ocean of compassion, having consoled the terrified and prostrate Mahendra, caused him to cast off his terrible intoxication with gambling, women, drink, and hunting.
This very demon Pramāthin, created by the enraged sage, dwells within the hearts of embodied beings, bound by the qualities (guṇas) in the form of a pillar. // 6.28 //

In silence among the illustrious, in the motionless gaze of those of increased power, in the knitting of brows and facial distortions of the wealthy, and in the pair of eyebrows of the parasites and the like. // 6.29 //
On the tongues of those skilled in diplomacy, on the teeth, garments, and hair of the beautiful, on the lips of physicians, and on the necks of virtuous ministers and astrologers; (6.30)
Upon the shoulders of the brave warriors, in the hearts of the merchants, in the hands of the artisans,
upon the necks and the bending fingers of the students, and upon the breasts of the young women.
In their bellies they bore the likeness of those worthy of ancestral offerings; in their shanks, that of the men who carry messages;
in their temples, that of elephants; in their plumage, that of peacocks; and in their gait, that of swans.

Thus, this one named Madana, a stubborn obsession of intoxication and a firm delusion consisting of many transformations, dwells always within the bodies of all living beings as something petrified into wood. (6.33)
Thus ends the sixth canto, titled "The Description of Intoxication," in the *Kalāvilāsa* composed by the great poet Śrī Kṣemendra.
Canto 7: The Description of Singers.
Wealth is indeed the life-force of people, for it is the foundation of the entire range of their activities.
Even that, the most cunning singers with smooth throats carry away in this world. (7.1)
Having devoured the entire store of lotuses and tasted the night-lilies,
the bees who sing their songs grow emaciated and seek the company of elephants.
With shoulders like jars, cloths, and carts, and with many children and disheveled hair, these singers in the world are but piśācas born from a womb, though they are lords of the earth. (7.3)
In the darkness, the wretched thief flees in terror with cries of "Alas!
Alas!", whereas the singing thief openly robs one of all one's possessions while making those very same cries.
Having fashioned this row of notes and words—*pā pā dha dha ni ni ga ma sā dhā dhā mā mā sa mā sa gā dhā mā*—these musical rogues go about their way. (7.5)
With whirling, crooked gyrations, and with various changes of dress and facial expressions,
the troupe of singers sings for a long time while the drummer remains silent, his hands upon the drum.

With cries of "Hail! and shouts of victory, with the deep, gurgling sounds of the syllable *huṃ* uttered at every step, and with spontaneous exclamations of "Well done!", the singer drowned out the song.
If a grain of flour falls into water and is eaten by fish, there is some attainment of merit;
however, even for tens of millions of gifts given to singers, there is not even a trace of fruit.
For those whose wealth has been stolen by fate and confined within the depths of blind wells,
he has fashioned a flood of conduits called "singers" with their mouths wide open.
"It is not that these singing rogues always sing with their teeth bared; these rogues laugh at those who have grasped the meaning, following whatever path others have gone. (7.10)
In the morning, these rogues who sing for a living appear wise, adorned with bracelets and armlets;
at midday, defeated at gambling, they are naked, broken, and without support.
Bound by the snares of praise, with arrows of speech and the construction of deceptive traps, singers plunder the entire wealth of the innocent deer through their songs. 7.12.
Having in an instant gained hundreds of thousands through songs whose notes and words were lost, the singer goes away dejected, saying, "What was given by the son of a slave? (7.13)

This very curse was pronounced upon Lakṣmī by the virtuous, excellent brahmins, and elders, who were themselves bereft of them and overwhelmed with grief: that she should always be the food of singers. 7.14
Long ago, the Lord of the gods, the sovereign of the Suras, questioned Nārada— who had arrived after a long time— concerning the affairs of the world and the kings upon the earth.
"While wandering through the world of men, I have seen the splendors worthy of the Lord of the Gods belonging to victorious kings who perform many sacrifices of charity and dharma. (7.16)
They indeed vie with you in their splendors, surpassing Varuṇa, the lord of wealth, and even Indra—known as Śatamakha—by means of their many sacrifices, which they perform repeatedly. (7.17)
Having heard those words of the sage, Śatakratu became filled with hatred; out of anger, he dispatched Piśācas to the earth to seize the wealth of the kings.
Commanded by the Lord of the Gods, those hosts of Piśācas, whose names were songs and mantras,
set out for the surface of the earth to seize all the wealth of every king.
Māyādāsa was the first, followed by Ḍambaradāsa, Vajradāsa, Jh[kṣ?]ayadāsa, Luṇṭhadāsa, Kharaharadāsa, and Prasiddhadāsa. (7.20)
And those eight Vāḍava slaves, having gone to the mortal world which is exceedingly terrifying,
with their mouths wide open like dreadful caverns, produced an extremely grotesque creation of singers.

By these [demons], whose wealth has been plundered in every direction and who have seized all the possessions of the entire world, all kings have become slack in their efforts regarding sacrifices and other rites. (7.22)
For these most terrible ear-demons, entering through the openings of the ears under the guise of song, suddenly steal away the hearts of kings. (7.23)
Therefore, he who does not grant entry into his kingdom to these corrupters possesses a land that yields all prosperity, like a field tended by a wise man. (7.24)
Actors, dancers, wandering performers, bards, minstrels, and jesters—these are like locusts to one possessed of power; one should guard one's prosperity against them. (7.25)
From the unity of the assembly of singers, a very great sound of song arises,
like the frantic cry of fortune when it has been bestowed upon an unworthy place.
There too were goldsmiths, masters of the art of extraction and profound in their contemplation, who indeed demonstrated the emptiness within that abode of abundant splendor. (8.1)
The essence of all riches, an ornament in prosperity, and a protection in adversity—
these wicked ones constantly steal the supreme luster of gold.
The ever-impure and sinful Caṇḍālas and goldsmiths suddenly defile gold with their touch, causing its luster to be marred. (8.3)
The quality of those [gems] that undergoes a gradual decline in brilliance when tested on a smooth touchstone is itself their profit when sold on a rough touchstone.

One who is moistened with oil should be fomented using a vessel made primarily of sand, sealed with beeswax; and one who possesses internal heat should be treated according to the specific method, using five parts of the ingredients consisting of lead and tin.

The crucible has two layers, ripens with eruptions, drinks the essence of gold, possesses the quality of fine copper, is intent on taking up lead, dross, and powdered glass, and consists of six parts. (8.6)
With a curved mouth, uneven lips, and a hollow base, filled with mercury, soft, with side-wings, knotted, coated with beeswax, possessing many virtues, and bowed forward. // 8.7 //
Whether fluttering in the wind, slender or heavy, or reduced to powder by harsh winds—
whether lifeless or still living— these are sixteen parts of a tula of gold.
Slow, with agitation, interrupted in the middle, accompanied by a sound and a hissing,
falling, and creating droplets— these are the six qualities of their hissing.
Smoke that forms a circle of flames, crackles, is slow-moving, and emits sparks—
when these are combined with the previously mentioned copper powder, fire is produced from them in six parts.
Questioning, varied conversation, scratching, pulling at the hem of her garment, gazing at the sun at the time of day, excessive laughter, and the swatting away of flies. (8.11)
Beholding curiosities repeatedly, quarreling with one's own kin, breaking water-vessels, and going outside many times—these are their twelve activities during the twelfth lunar day. (8.12)
The firing of a fused vessel enhances the manifestation of its artificial color by means of a coating of salt and alkali within a fire of thin cow-dung.
Even when placed upon the surface of magnetite set on the ground, a balance made of common iron repeatedly moves with its face toward it; though empty, it appears as if constantly full.
When the balance-beam is fixed and ready for use, a tiny particle of gold, having been surreptitiously inserted, can easily be extracted at the time of weighing. // 8.15 //

Moreover, their downfall would be very easy to accomplish even during a time of prosperity; and when they are adorned with similar and diverse ornaments, there is ease in their exchange and expansion. (8.16)

The taking of what is full, the joining together, the lack of observation, the offering of beans, the conjunction with light, the loss through the passing of time, the request for replenishment, and excessive attachment. // 8.17 //
For them, there are eleven periods of conjunction; briefly stated, all these, having taken up the entire night, constitute a single great digit. // 8.18 //
These sixty-four arts are obtainable through the deliberation of goldsmiths; other arts, however, remain hidden such that even the thousand-eyed Indra does not know them.
Meru stands at a great distance, having long since abandoned the realm of men, fearing the inevitable theft by the terrible goldsmiths. (8.20)
In the past, Mount Meru was hollowed out by mice, who carved away all its peaks with a multitude of millions of great cavities extending from the joints of hundreds of golden rocks.
In that place, Meru’s roots must surely have long since become loosened by the scratching and gouging of the claws of the entire army of mice as they burrowed beneath it. (8.22)
Dug up by the claws of mice, Mount Sumeru shone even more brightly;
the many directions were turned tawny by masses of rising golden dust.
On that dilapidated peak, where the slopes of its golden summit were revealed through the openings of its caverns,
a fear born of the apprehension that the end of the aeon had arrived manifested among the immortals.
