And having beheld all that with his divine vision, Agastya, the lord of the gods, said:
"These are those night-stalkers, slayers of Brahmins, who were slain in the battle of the thirty gods."
Having been born in the form of mice at Meru’s fall, they have begun their activity;
they are to be slain by you once again for destroying the hermitages of the sages.
Having heard these words of the sage, the gods filled the openings of the caves with smoke and devoured the great mice that had previously been burnt by the curse.
These very same goldsmiths have been born again on earth as these [monks];
through the habituation of their previous births, they incessantly rub the gold-dust. (8.28)
Therefore, in the absence of poisoners, thieves, and robbers, a single goldsmith should always be restrained by kings in every way. (8.29)
Canto 9: Description of Various Rogues On this entire earth, girdled by the ocean, the great artifice of deception is like a net spread by fishermen for fish whose intellects have perished. (9.1)
Those for whose sake this effort is made, who hold their very lives as their supreme treasure—they too must always be known by physicians who remain at their disposal. 9.2
For these physicians, like unbearable separations following the burning of the body, or like fierce summer days, utterly wither one through their many cravings. (9.3)
Having killed a thousand men through various applications of medicinal herbs in order to test his own knowledge, he subsequently becomes a perfected physician. // 9.4 //
Having set out the wheel of the zodiac, he mimics the calculation of the planets with contortions of his face,
repeating whatever has been said by the judge after a long time.
The astrologer calculates in the sky the conjunction of the moon with Viśākhā, yet he does not know that his own wife is intent on various amorous sports with a serpent. // 9.6 //
First, desiring gold, he reduces his entire own wealth to ashes; afterwards, this deceitful man destroys wealthy connoisseurs as well. (9.7)
"My hundredfold transmuter is perfected; even the thousandfold transmuting elixir has emerged," says the alchemist, naked, filthy, emaciated, and coarse.
For the rogue who practices elixirs, his head resembling a copper pot and worn out by old age, deceives only those with bald heads by talking of hair restoration. (9.9)
Though he has fixed his hopes even upon the wives of Śambara, who were as enchanting as Prahlāda’s own daughter Śuci,
this man of excessive lust, having offered oblations of wood-apples and other fruits, falls into blindness from the smoke.
The sky-farers are easily attained; if a flower from the sky were obtained through effort, it would be so.
Thus have the experts in ritual applications stated that various accomplishments are found even within the bones of mosquitoes. (9.11)
By smearing oneself with the dung of a black horse, one sees the palaces of the lords of the gods in the sky;
by being anointed with the fat of a frog, a man becomes beloved of the apsarases.
Having spoken thus, the throngs of rogues again sport in every direction,
by whom hundreds of men, greedy for various supernatural powers, have been cast into the abyss.
The practitioner of subjugation and attraction provides protection for women at every step, yet he does not know the root mantra—the root of the *ratikāma-tantra*. (9.14)
Many who are teachers of the path, having received only a brief initiation, produce a mere semblance of yoga and thrive like hunters, seizing the wealth and wives of the simple-minded. (9.15)
"Her line of wealth on the hand is exceedingly broad, yet her husband will be fickle-minded;
he will oppress these women of noble family," saying this, she [pressed] her hand, soft as a lotus.
When her thumb is submerged in water, a young girl sees various delusions of people; yet the thief is not caught—this is the illusion of a magician’s trick.
The rogue eats and drinks while making people babble with claps of his palms, having induced a state of possession in the servant by means of incantation-free, trivial incense. (9.18)
"Let the formula written by Nāgārjuna be applied to the incense in the pouch;
for that rogue, out of delusion, throws another's wealth into the fire in order to steal it. (9.19)
The sons of Yakṣīs should be known as thieves who manufacture counterfeit incense; their manifest fruit is poverty and ruin at the hands of the king. (9.20)
By means of talk such as "that daughter has been taken by my son" or "she is under my control," the merchant with abundant wealth makes the rogue consume the girl's dowry. (9.21)
One who speaks of his own gestures must be considered a knower of one's vital secrets and a thief of the heart;
employed by another, he remains either falsely pretending to be deaf or mute. (9.22)
Prostitutes, old women, female ascetics, and female deities—these courtesans wander among noblewomen, stealing their wealth and virtue. (9.23)
A young widow, though possessing wealth, desires a divine lover such as yourself;
yet the rogue, calling her "foolish," consumes all of her property. (9.24)
Those who, though appointed with daily wages for their tasks, are deceitful craftsmen who sport about by creating obstacles to work—they are to be known as "thieves of time. (9.25)
Skilled in various deceptive methods of gambling, such as mental calculation and manual dexterity, these clever rogues roam incognito as renowned gamblers in foreign lands.

One who produces only enough food for himself yet incurs great expenditure through gambling, liquor, and prostitutes should be known as a house-thief, whether he be a kinsman or a domestic servant. (9.27)
"He who says, 'A composed scripture is untrue, and by whom has the next world been directly seen?'—he is to be feared like an unrestrained, intoxicated elephant. (9.28)
Those who, being highly cunning, seize the wealth of others with unbearable gain while their own minds are greedy for abundant profit— these should be known as thieves of gain.

In the midst of the ocean of legal disputes, those known as Bhaṭṭas— who are thieves of justice and whose minds are fixated on wealth and people— are like submarine fires that burn with constant consumption.

Those who are bees at the lotus of worldly prosperity, who turn their backs on the forceful gales of unbearable calamity, and who wander about summoned by the creeper of fortune—such friends are actually thieves of one's happiness. (9.31)
Whatever he previously practiced, even if it was disconnected from conceptual thought, he describes it in many words as something that causes delight; such a person is a "thief of the ear. (9.32)
Those who, having generated faith in faults through praises of virtues, create a new fabrication by means of fourfold speech, are thieves of the established order and devoid of proper conduct. 9.33

Those supreme rogues, who are thieves of virtue, intent on proclaiming their own qualities while concealing the qualities of others with great effort, prevail over those whose hearts are deluded. (9.34)
Those rogues who, having attained the state of being favorites, destroy the favor of others through various kinds of slander— they are thieves of livelihood driven by envy.
Devoid of tranquility, self-control, and devotion, and seized by the obsession with intense vows, this thief of reputation surpasses virtuous people through his practice. (9.36)
Even those who, like thieves of their own country, lead others abroad with descriptions of the delights found in other lands—delights that are merely pleasant to hear—are but beasts. (9.37)

Through various transformations of laughter and many displays of cleverness, he—who steals away the functions of one's very nature—delights [her] for the entirety of the day with his skill in deceiving her. (9.38)

One should reflect upon those parasites whose own abundant wealth has been consumed, who are consecrated to the destruction of others' riches, and whose mouths are incessantly vocal with praise for the brothels of courtesans. (9.39)
Because of his extreme purity, he does not accept wealth and performs the highest office;
he is a fish in the waters of restraint, a disinterested official who must be avoided [by the worldly].
Whatever wicked shopkeepers on the street bring to one's own home and offer, even if it were merely a fragment of glass, it all becomes as if placed directly into one’s own hand. (9.41)
Those who follow one's will, who are intent on speaking well even when falling into a pit, and who seize all one's possessions—these sweet ones enter within like poison. (9.42)
"Your king is gracious and intent upon counting your virtues; yet, having spoken thus in private, he has always been robbed of his servants by the royal attendants. (9.43)
"In a dream, I saw Śrī, lotus-in-hand, enter your house; that goddess Śrī, pleased by my month-long fast, spoke respectfully. (9.44)
"He will give you all the truth obtained by me through my devotion"—having said this, rogues sport in every house among the simple-minded. (9.45)

In crowds of people gathered for occasions such as the destruction of a city, the founding of a new city, sacrifices, weddings, or festivals, even strangers disguised as kinsmen enter for the purpose of plundering everything. (9.46)
On occasions when his attendants drink, he does not drink wine; he keeps watch during the nights, intent on meditation, seeking service and making every effort to perform some task. (9.47)
He does not give an answer, or he gives one with faltering syllables and unevenly;
with his face lost and gasping for breath, the thief trembles at that very moment. (9.48)
He who desires excessive purity, he who speaks with arrogance, and he who practices terrible denial—that sinful person shall be a source of suspicion. // 9.49 //
He who, remaining unchanging, treats as unperformed what has been performed and as unsaid what has been said— whether witnessed or out of sight— is the supreme object of fear for men.
He who wanders among women with a feigned innocence, like a eunuch whose conversation is full of feminine affectations—he is the rogue Kāmadeva in the house. (9.51)
One who constantly keeps his gaze downward in the treasury house should be suspected as a mouse;
one who scratches [the ground] while appointed to the treasury house should be suspected as a mouse in the treasury house. // 9.52 //
That servant who remains all day long in the pleasure-houses of the home, telling long-winded stories about domestic affairs—he must be abandoned with one's whole soul. // 9.53 //

He who, in every way, deceives others in blameworthy actions that deserve heavy punishment, has bound for himself a stable mass of food to be consumed throughout his life out of fear for his livelihood. (9.54)
Having observed his secret in its entirety and having effortlessly discovered his hidden motive,
that rogue inscribed the bewildered world upon a stone slab.
A rogue, for the purpose of destroying wealthy men, deposits property, goods, forged documents, or something else that is contrary to the king's interests, and then departs unobserved. (9.56)

By him who, though mean and impoverished, was made to find enjoyment in his home through wealth, that very man—holding weapons, poison, and nooses in his hands—was held captive by means of those same nooses. (9.57)

One who possesses the wealth of modesty, is of noble birth, and is esteemed for his pure conduct and moral boundaries, is generally reduced to the state of a woman by rogues, especially by women with child. (9.58)
With glances, both seen and unseen, and with cruel signs and feigned words, the rogue deceives his innocent bride while her husband is away on a journey. (9.59)

Even in the presence of virtuous people, rogues wearing the dress of holy men and adorned with ornaments may, with ease, steal everything from the steadfast; yet, when seen through, they meet only with laughter and no gain.

Having established a prosperous household in a flourishing region and filled it with wealth through ostentatious displays, the rogue Kumbhadhana flees after a year, having stolen a hundred thousand pieces deposited with him. // 9.61 //
Adorned with bodies and garments of exceedingly pure gold, rogues are honored with great excitement in every house under the pretext of being princes defeated by enemies. (9.62)
Having taken the virtuous goat, a bull among gods, sold by the rogue, the joy arising from a profitable gain turned into a bitter fruit of suffering for the simple-minded one. (9.63)
The abandonment of wealth by the great even amidst prosperity, accompanied by reproach toward one who has become envious—
that is why he, though empty-handed, gives his riches with effort out of fear.
Having formed a great caravan with worthless bhr̥ja-wood, the rogue wanders in every direction and robs thousands of wood-gatherers. 9.65 //
A rogue residing in foreign lands, under the pretext of a pilgrimage to the Ganges and Gayā, takes wealth from the simple-minded for the sake of deceased kinsmen. (9.66)
The woman of the caravan plunders those who are deluded by sleep, taking their garments; yet even she is deceived at night by the rogue who gives her a counterfeit coin.
Having cast a deaf man, a madman, or a mad merchant into the warehouse, the rogue quickly carries off the highly valuable coloring substances. (9.68)
With a mere modicum of familiarity, a touch of audacity, some conceptualizations, and a bit of dispute and quarrel, the self-styled "omniscient" one wanders about as a deceiver. (9.69)
A rogue who is wealthy through false pretenses, a scholar by means of books, one who possesses knowledge only in stories, a hero in mere description, fickle, and four-faced, flourishes. (9.70)
Having abandoned those with whom he had made a pact by shaking all his limbs as a signal, that great rogue, acting according to his own will, goes to the ends of the earth to eat in private houses.
"Having eaten an āmalaka fruit that is a hundred years old, I have arrived from Śrīparvata"; thus the rogue says before his teachers, "I am mindful of omens. (9.72)
These sixty-four illusions have been described by me only in brief;
who can know the hundreds of thousands of illusions belonging to deceivers?
Thus ends the ninth canto, titled "The Description of Various Rogues," in the *Kalāvilāsa* composed by the great poet Śrī Kṣemendra.
Canto 10.
These are to be understood as deceptive illusions and should not be practiced oneself;
this collection of arts pertaining to dharma is desired by the wise for the sake of prosperity. 10.1
The supreme constituent of Dharma is known as compassion for all beings, as well as benevolence toward others;
[the rest are] generosity, patience, freedom from envy, truthfulness, lack of greed, and clarity of mind. (10.2)
Constant exertion for wealth, observance of discipline, knowledge of action, abandoning one's place, cleverness, freedom from agitation, and lack of trust in women. // 10.3 //
The beauty of dress, gracefulness, loveliness, excellence of virtue, various playful gestures, and knowledge of the hearts of beloved women—these are the attributes of desire. (10.4)
Delight in discernment, tranquility, the destruction of craving, contentment, renunciation of attachment, abiding in the self, and the light of supreme wisdom—these are the means to liberation. 10.5

These four groups of eight digits, whether held in their sequential order or all together, constitute the Vidyā for those who possess knowledge and for those who have deceived the cycle of existence. 10.6.
The renunciation of stinginess, pleasant speech, fortitude, freedom from anger, and detachment for the sake of others—these five are the perfected arts of happiness. 10.7.

Association with the virtuous, mastery over desire, purity, constant attendance upon the guru, right conduct, stainless learning, and delight in fame—these are the seven root arts of moral discipline. 10.8.
Vigor, courage, intelligence, resolve, statesmanship, discernment of gestures, confidence, good companions, gratitude, secrecy in counsel, and generosity. (10.9)
Devotion, practical application, winning friends, compassion, lack of arrogance, and affection for those who depend on one—these are the seventeen qualities of majesty. 10.10.
Silence, lack of greed, and not begging—this triad of arts is the very life of self-respect;
these sixty-four arts should be cultivated within oneself by the wise.
When one's power is thwarted, one should depart or bow down; when power arises, one should pursue enmity.
For the afflicted, there is the practice of Dharma; in suffering, fortitude; and in pleasures, the absence of pride. (10.12)
Sharing one's wealth, delighting in the virtuous, wisdom regarding doubts concerning mantras, and turning away from what is blameworthy—this is the tenfold medicine for the arts. 10.13.
The word of the guru is the foremost among truths; the worship of cows, the twice-born, and the gods is the foremost among duties;
greed is the most sinful of vices; and anger is the greatest generator of all afflictions. (10.14)
O wise one, among all virtues, fame is the most excellent; among vast riches, service is the most painful; and among hopes, the snares of the great black serpent are the most terrifying.
Generosity is the source of treasures; freedom from enmity is the source of regions of happiness; begging is the destroyer of pride; and poverty is the cause of affliction. (10.16)

Dharma is the path for those traveling on a journey; truth is that which purifies the lotus-face; calamity is the foremost among hosts of diseases; and laziness is the destroyer of domestic prosperity. (10.17)

Freedom from desire is the mark of those who are praiseworthy; pleasant speech, of those who are entirely sweet; pride, of those who cause the darkness of delusion; and hypocrisy, of those who are objects of universal derision. (10.18)
Freedom from malice is the foremost among purities; lack of fickleness is the best of specific vows and observances;
refraining from backbiting is the best of unpleasant things; and not cutting off others' livelihoods is the best of cruel deeds. // 10.19 //
Compassion is the mark of meritorious deeds; gratitude is the sign of true men; deceit belongs to those of deluded minds; and ingratitude is the cause for falling into hell.

Madana is the foremost among wandering thieves; the word of women is the foremost among causes of division among kinsmen; the cruel are the foremost among caṇḍālas; and the deceitful are the foremost among the advents of the Kali age.
The treatises are but lamps for jewels; the instructions are but consecrations; old age is but the afflictions; and sickness is but suffering equal to death. (10.22)
Affection is the poison of those with uneven horns; a courtesan’s passion is the leprosy of spreading sores;
a wife is the essence of household wealth; and a son is the kinsman for the world beyond.

An enemy is the foremost among hundreds of thorns; a wicked son is the foremost among the destroyers of a lineage; youth is the foremost among women; and beauty is the foremost among graceful manners and attire. (10.24)

Contentment is superior to kingdoms; association with the virtuous is superior to the splendors of a universal monarch; reflection is superior to things that cause emaciation; and freedom from hatred is superior to the fires burning within hollow trees. // 10.25 //

Loving-kindness is the absence of constraint among those who are trustworthy; it is the contraction of costly enjoyments, the reduction of diseases, and the crookedness of waterless, dark wells. // 10.26 //
Uprightness belongs to those whose hands are stainless; humility to those crowned with the jewels of excellence;
gambling to those with evil addictions; and being conquered by women to those who are goblins haunting the mountain ridges.
The casting off of jeweled bracelets, the removal of bright ear-jewels from the ears,
the friendship of the wicked, and service to the fickle— these are all futile labors.

Nirvāṇa is the best of gardens; the sight of the beloved is a rain of nectar; delight in the truth is the best of attainments; and the assembly of fools is the destruction of right discernment. // 10.29 //
Noble birth is the good fortune of fruitful trees; a royal family is the refuge of those worthy of honor; and a woman's heart is the natural seat of crookedness. (10.30)
Propriety belongs to those worthy of praise; passion for virtues belongs to those who anoint themselves with sandalwood and the like;
lack of intelligence belongs to those who cause grief to maidens; and compassion belongs to those who are to be pitied. (10.31)
Prosperity is the source of good fortunes, public affection is the root of fame, wine is the haunt of Vetālas, and hunting is the lair of yakṣas in the elephant-thickets.

Tranquility is the foremost among things that bring well-being; delight in the self is the best among pilgrimages; greed is the worst among things devoid of fruit; and the lack of moral conduct is the worst among places of cremation.
The protection of women is the foremost among policies; the conquest of the senses is the foremost among powers;
jealousy is the foremost among hundreds of diseases; and infamy is the foremost among deaths by leprosy.
The mother is the source of all auspicious things; the father is the originator of festivals for meritorious deeds;
[the body] is the whetstone for the sharpest [virtues] and the whetted edge of sharp swords.
Prostration is the foremost among those things that remove resentment; friendship is the foremost among those things requested in times of distress;
pride is the foremost among those things that bring nourishment; and fame is the foremost among those things that constitute the essence of worldly existence.

Devotion to the Lord is the path to happiness for those led [by it]; death in battle is the path to bliss; discipline is the source of all auspicious things; and enthusiasm is the source of all accomplishments.
Merit belongs to those most worthy of attainment; knowledge belongs to those of supreme illumination;
and in this saṃsāra, fame is the most essential thing for all people. (10.38)
He should be known as one skilled in the entire range of arts, a knower of the reality of all things, and the most excellent in this world, like a brahmin among all the social classes. // 10.39 //

Thus it has been said: for one who knows these hundred subtle portions of the arising of the auspicious and inauspicious, prosperity—seen to serve practical purposes—is observed in their very worldly dealings. (10.40)
Having spoken thus and dismissed his disciples after performing the appropriate rites, Mūladeva spent the night in his own palace, which was like a blossoming cluster of rays.

May this *Kalāvilāsa*, delightful with the arts of playful smiles, a manifest lamp revealing the inner arts that serve as the refuge for all, a subject of instruction for the world, and variegated with beautiful narratives, be dear to the virtuous. (10.42)
May *Kalāvilāsa*, emerging from the ocean of Kṣemendra’s creative genius, constantly bring joy to the minds of the virtuous, like the moon. (10.43)
Thus ends the tenth canto, titled "The Description of All Arts," in the *Kalāvilāsa* composed by the great poet Śrī Kṣemendra.
